title: Disney Expected to Lay Off Thousands of Staffers in Biggest Round of Cuts This Year
description: Disney is gearing up for a significant round of layoffs, with some managers told to cut expenses by 20% on an annualized basis, Bloomberg News repo
body:
Disney is gearing up for a significant round of layoffs, with some managers told to cut expenses by 20% on an annualized basis, Bloomberg News reported.

	It would be the fourth round of job cuts in 2026 under Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro and affect the most number of staffers. The Bloomberg report, which cited anonymous sources, said some Disney operations “will be affected disproportionately,” but it did not provide details on which areas would suffer the brunt of the cutbacks. D’Amaro “aims to reinvest a portion of the savings into film and TV programming, technology and the theme parks and cruise ship businesses,” according to the report.
	

	Disney declined to comment.

	Disney has been planning a major restructuring of its TV operations, which would eliminate hundreds of jobs and consolidate divisions, the Wall Street Journal reported last month.

	In late September, Disney let go a few hundred employees, primarily in its human resources and IT departments across corporate and within different divisions. In July, Disney made job cuts eliminating several hundred jobs across certain corporate functions, including at Pixar, ESPN, Disney Entertainment Television and Disney’s studios. And in April, the Mouse House eliminated about 1,000 roles, primarily as a result of D’Amaro’s formation of a consolidated enterprise marketing division under the leadership of Asad Ayaz, chief marketing and brand officer.

	Dana Walden, Disney’s president and chief creative officer, addressed the most recent Disney layoffs at the Bloomberg Screentime event last month. “I think, like all of our similarly situated competitors, and certainly all of our competitors in the tech industry, there is a need to constantly evaluate how you’re structured,” Walden said. 
	

	In August, Disney offered early-retirement buyout packages to longtime executives, as part of its ongoing cost-cutting efforts. That offer was available to U.S.-based employees at the director through EVP levels within the Disney Entertainment, ESPN and corporate divisions, with a minimum age of 50 and at least 10 years of service. 

	About the voluntary buyout offers, Walden said at the Bloomberg conference that the program “was extremely generous and gave a number of our long-tenured executives agency and the opportunity to make their own decisions around whether the timing was right to leave or to stay, knowing that this evolution will never stop, technology set their sights on our business, and we must survive and thrive and grow, and that’s what we’re going to do.”

	In announcing results for the June 2026 quarter, D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston had indicated that additional job cuts were coming. “We remain highly focused on reducing costs across the enterprise to create incremental capacity to invest for growth and are evaluating a variety of levers, including reductions in labor and SG&A [selling, general and administrative expenses],” the execs wrote in the Aug. 5 letter to Disney shareholders.

	Disney is scheduled to report results for the September quarter, the company’s Q4 of fiscal 2026, on Nov. 17 before the market opens.

	Other media companies are making job cuts, too. Netflix last month axed about 1,000 workers, and Skydance — the company formed via the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery — is expected to make significant layoffs by the end of the year.

schema.headline: Disney Expected to Lay Off Thousands of Staffers in Biggest Round of Cuts This Year

title: Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross to Score David Fincher’s ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’
description: Nine Inch Nails principals and veteran film composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross are once again teaming up to provide the score for David Finche
body:
Nine Inch Nails principals and veteran film composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross are once again teaming up to provide the score for David Fincher‘s new film “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” marking their sixth collaboration with Fincher on one of his movies.

	News of Reznor and Ross’ score was revealed on the poster for the film, which will be released exclusively to IMAX on November 25 for two weeks before it becomes available to stream on Netflix beginning on December 23. The duo first worked with Fincher on 2010’s “The Social Network,” winning the Academy Award and Golden Globe for best original score.
	

	Reznor and Ross continued to provide music for all of Fincher’s subsequent films including 2011’s “The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo,” 2014’s “Gone Girl,” 2020’s “Mank” and 2023’s “The Killer.” In 2013, they won the Grammy for best score soundtrack for visual media for “Girl With the Dragon Tattoo.”

	Outside of their work with Fincher, Reznor and Ross have composed the scores for numerous films including “Patriots Day,” “Soul,” “Challengers,” “Bird Box” and “Queer.” Ross has been collaborating with Reznor as far back as 2002, when they worked on the project Tapeworm, and has contributed to numerous Nine Inch Nails releases.

	“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is a spin-off of 2019’s “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” focusing on Brad Pitt’s title character. The film, written by Quentin Tarantino, is set eight years after the events of “Hollywood” and features an ensemble cast that includes Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Timothy Olyphant and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II.

title: Neve Campbell Confirms Return for ‘Scream 8’
description:
Sidney Prescott will return for “Scream 8.” 

	Neve Campbell confirmed that she will reprise her role as the ultimate final girl after Sidney survi
body:
Sidney Prescott will return for “Scream 8.” 

	Neve Campbell confirmed that she will reprise her role as the ultimate final girl after Sidney survived her latest run-in with the Ghostface-masked killers in “Scream 7.”

	The 2025 movie was a major box office success, tallying the 30-year-old franchise’s biggest opening ever ($97.2 million worldwide) and ultimately becoming the series’ highest-grossing installment ($208 million worldwide against a $45 million budget). As a result, Spyglass Media and Paramount Pictures, which distributes the films, quickly began developing “Scream 8.”
	

	Campbell confirmed her involvement on Monday during an interview with the Associated Press, promoting her role in the Netflix series “Black Doves.”

	“‘Scream 8.’ That’s in the pipeline as well,” Campbell said, listing the meta-horror movie among her upcoming projects. When pressed for further details about what Sidney will face this time around, she demurred. “You know I can’t tell you anything about Scream 8,” Campbell said, laughing. “I’ll be in it.”

	Campbell has starred in six out of the seven “Scream” movies, taking a break for 2023’s “Scream 6” following a contract dispute. She returned for “Scream 7” after receiving a reported $7 million salary to play Sidney again.

	At the time, she told CBS Mornings that she “didn’t think I could live with myself” if she accepted the offer to return for “Scream 6” knowing that her “value to this franchise was bigger than what had been offered.” “I just didn’t feel right.. For me, I needed to make that choice,” she said. 
	

	In 2022, Campbell told Variety that she would not be returning for the sixth installment because she felt “the offer that was presented to me did not equate to the value I have brought to the franchise.”

title: New Japanese Animation Prize Named Nippon Anime Awards, Sets First Ceremony for November 2027
description: A new Japanese anime awards program will be called the Nippon Anime Awards, with the first ceremony set for Nov. 21, 2027, at SGC Hall Ariake in To
body:
A new Japanese anime awards program will be called the Nippon Anime Awards, with the first ceremony set for Nov. 21, 2027, at SGC Hall Ariake in Tokyo’s Ariake district.

	The Association of Japanese Animations (AJA), the industry body behind the prize, announced the name on Nov. 2 at Tokyo Tatemono Brillia Hall. The reveal closed out Tokyo Anime Next, a program of screenings, workshops and live shows that ran Oct. 30–Nov. 2, mostly in Tokyo’s Ikebukuro neighborhood.
	

	AJA president Ishikawa Kazuko unveiled the name on stage alongside the awards’ slogan, “Moving Frames. Moving Hearts. Moving the World.” The awards will honor standout anime titles and the people who make them, with an eye on audiences both in Japan and overseas. The ceremony will also host initiatives, run with the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, aimed at opening up new business for the animation sector and developing young talent.

	In a message shared at the event, Tokyo Governor Koike Yuriko said: “The Tokyo Metropolitan Government will continue to provide strong support for anime and everyone involved in bringing it to life.”

	The announcement capped a roughly 90-minute main event. Its second half, the Orchestra Premium Stage, set the Tokyo Philharmonic Orchestra against specially cut footage from three anime series. Nakagawa Nami sang “Kamado Tanjiro no Uta” for the “Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba” segment, which also featured an orchestral take on the score cue “Demon Slayer Corps.” Higuchi Ai performed “Akuma no Ko,” the closing theme of “Attack on Titan: The Final Season Part 2,” after the orchestra played “Ashes on the Fire.”
	

	The finale went to “Detective Conan,” which is marking its 30th anniversary. Kuraki Mai, who has recorded numerous songs for the series, performed “Secret of My Heart” backed by the orchestra.

	“We hope to share the appeal and potential of anime to an even wider audience around the world and build that future together with all of you,” Ishikawa said.

	The evening opened with a panel on anime’s international pull. It featured comedian Itakura Toshiyuki of the duo Impulse, singer Nakagawa Shoko and Sally Amaki of 22/7. Amaki, who was raised in Los Angeles, revealed that her entry point into anime music was Nakagawa Shoko’s “Sorairo Days,” the opening theme of “Gurren Lagann.” She added that she had sung it at her audition to become a voice actor.

	“I’m so glad I became an anime singer,” Nakagawa Shoko said.

	Elsewhere across the four days, a symposium at The Tokyo International Film Festival‘s TIFFCOM market on Oct. 30 examined the purpose of the new awards. Over the following weekend, 14 titles, most of them theatrical features, screened at three Ikebukuro cinemas, with cast and crew talk sessions attached to four of them. The lineup also gave “Lona,” a TV series from screenwriter Nogi Akiko and Wit Studio, its world premiere with a screening of episode one.

	Production classes at Toshima Civic Center brought in staff from “Cosmic Princess Kaguya!” and “Mobile Suit Gundam Hathaway: The Sorcery of Nymph Circe.” The program also included a session on a Japan-Saudi Arabia co-produced animation made for Saudi Arabia’s 96th National Day. Children were given studio light tables to trace frames from “Chibi-Maruko-chan.”

	Tokyo Anime Next was organized by the AJA and co-organized by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, with Toshima City as special sponsor. Sony Music Solutions ran the event secretariat.

schema.headline: New Japanese Animation Prize Named Nippon Anime Awards, Sets First Ceremony for November 2027

title: New Indian Horror Lab Aims to Push Genre Past Ghosts and Comedy Hybrids (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
A new screenwriting lab in India wants to steer the country’s horror films away from ghost stories and horror-comedy hybrids. 

	Independent outfit
body:
A new screenwriting lab in India wants to steer the country’s horror films away from ghost stories and horror-comedy hybrids. 

	Independent outfit Platoon One Films will pick 15 writers for a three-month program built around original genre scripts.

	The Platoon One Horror Lab will run entirely online, and each of the 15 participants will bring an original horror screenplay to develop. Sessions will take place on weekends and will be led by seasoned screenwriters and directors from India and other countries. The format mixes group mentoring, discussions on craft and individual sessions on each script, so that writers get ongoing feedback as their drafts evolve.
	

	When the lab wraps, participants will get the chance to pitch their projects to producers and other industry figures through Platoon One’s network, which could lead to financing and, eventually, a shoot. The company will name the program’s mentors and faculty in the next few weeks.

	“We can talk about much bigger, philosophical and metaphysical ideas through horror, and sometimes it is far more powerful than simply expressing them through dialogue,” said Shiladitya Bora, founder of Platoon One Films. “What attracts me to the genre is often the messaging beneath the surface. Horror allows you to explore things that are difficult to confront directly.”

	The company said much of India’s mainstream horror keeps returning to the same supernatural staples and predictable beats, even though the country’s myths, folk tales and local beliefs offer far richer material. The lab will push writers to use the genre as a lens on society and the human mind, and to learn how suspense and atmosphere are built.
	

	“I wanted to start this lab because I feel we need to understand the genre better and bring genuinely good horror stories to our audiences,” Bora said. “Frankly, I was getting tired of watching horror-comedies that were neither scary nor funny. We have such a rich storytelling culture, and I believe there is so much more we can do with horror.”

	Platoon One’s wider goal is to help Indian horror travel. The company pictured tales that might start in an Indian hamlet yet still frighten viewers in Seoul or São Paulo.

	“I see this as an opportunity to help create the next generation of writers and filmmakers who can take Indian horror to a whole new level,” Bora said.

	Platoon One Films is an indie production and distribution company that also handles international sales and creative development.

schema.headline: New Indian Horror Lab Aims to Push Genre Past Ghosts and Comedy Hybrids (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Elena Maganini, Film Editor on ‘Dexter,’ ‘Henry, Portrait of a Serial Killer,’ Dies at 70
description: Elena Maganini, a TV and film editor who won an Emmy for cutting the pilot for “Dexter” and edited several films for director John McNaughton, died
body:
Elena Maganini, a TV and film editor who won an Emmy for cutting the pilot for “Dexter” and edited several films for director John McNaughton, died Oct. 21 in Burbank of complications from breast cancer. She was 70. 

	Born in Chicago, she graduated from the U. of Illinois and studied filmmaking at Columbia College in Chicago. Maganini started out working at Sinnot & Associates, a Chicago production company. 


	Her first feature credit came for McNaughton’s influential 1986 “Henry, Portrait of a Serial Killer.” She went on to edit McNaughton films including “Wild Things,” which starred Matt Dillon, Neve Campbell and Kevin Bacon, “Mad Dog & Glory” and “Sex, Drugs and Rock & Roll,” “The Borrower,” “Speaking of Sex” and “Lansky.” Other feature credits include “Next Friday” and “Ed Gein.” 
	

	Moving into television, Maganini edited the pilot for “Dexter,” for which she won an Emmy, and went on to edit shows including “Madam Secretary,” “Good Behavior,” “Clarice,” “Manifest” and “The Cleaning Lady.” She was nominated for an Emmy and a Cable ACE Award for “If These Walls Could Talk,” an anthology about abortion directed by Cher and Nancy Savoca and starring Catherine Keener, Demi Moore and Shirley Knight. 

	She was a member of American Cinema Editors.

	Survivors include husband Scott Collins, communications director at Motion Picture Editors Guild; daughter Gabriella Coronel; and daughter-in-law Adrienne Coronel.

	A memorial service will be held Nov. 15 at 1 p.m. at the Fine Arts Theatre in Beverly Hills.Donations may be made to Columbia College Chicago, Tree House Humane Society or the Stray Cat Alliance.

schema.headline: Elena Maganini, Film Editor on ‘Dexter,’ ‘Henry, Portrait of a Serial Killer,’ Dies at 70

title: Cynthia Nixon Says She ‘Loved’ Miranda’s Attempts to Become ‘Woke’ on ‘And Just Like That’ Despite Fans Being ‘Horrified’
description: Cynthia Nixon is standing by her “Sex and the City” character Miranda Hobbes’ arc in the chaotic reboot “And Just Like That” — despite how bewilder
body:
Cynthia Nixon is standing by her “Sex and the City” character Miranda Hobbes’ arc in the chaotic reboot “And Just Like That” — despite how bewildering some fans found it.

	In a recent interview with The New York Times, the actress explained that despite the fact that the show’s viewers “were so horrified by [Miranda’s] sadness and alcoholism and awkwardness at trying to become a woke person at this advanced age,” that was what she appreciated most about the character. “I loved that,” she said.
	

	While Hobbes underwent several personal shifts in the reboot of the iconic 6 Season HBO drama, the most contentious point for audiences was her relationship with comedian Che Diaz, whom she left her husband, Steve Brady, for in Season 1. In the original series, Hobbes, a lawyer, met Brady, a bartender, in Season 2, then broke up, ultimately got back together, got married, and welcomed a child, Brady Hobbes, by the show’s end.

	Nixon also spoke of how she was swayed to reprise the role of Hobbes in the reboot to begin with. “I became convinced that we could really do interesting, dangerous things,” she said. “And that we could make up for some of our past mistakes, the chief one being that it was such an overwhelmingly white show.” And while reactions to the show were always a mixed bag, Nixon admits she was caught off guard when she learned “And Just Like That” wouldn’t be returning for a fourth season: “I was not at all ready,” she said. “Not at all.”

	Currently, Nixon stars in HBO’s historical drama “The Gilded Age” as Ada Forte. The show debuted in Jan. 2022 and has run for three subsequent seasons. Season 4 premiered on Sunday on HBO and HBO Max.
	

	Despite the success of “The Gilded Age,” though, Nixon noted that “Miranda seems to eclipse everything else” she’s done, even 22 years after “Sex and the City” finished airing in 2004.

schema.headline: Cynthia Nixon Says She ‘Loved’ Miranda’s Attempts to Become ‘Woke’ on ‘And Just Like That’ Despite Fans Being ‘Horrified’

title: ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Director Matsubayashi Yoju on a 10-Year Journey Tracing Brazilian Dancers’ Island Roots
description: Exploring the relationship between people and place, new documentary “Okinawa Saudade,” playing at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival as pa
body:
Exploring the relationship between people and place, new documentary “Okinawa Saudade,” playing at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival as part of its Nippon Cinema Now selection, was born from director Matsubayashi Yoju’s time with a Brazilian community of Okinawan immigrants some 10 years ago.

	The film zooms in on the latest generation of Okinawan immigrant families: Yumi, a young dancer of Ryukyu Buyo, Okinawa’s classical dance, and Everton, who teaches Eisa, the island’s drum-led festival dance, in Brazil. The two travel to Okinawa on an exchange trip to learn about the island’s history and culture.
	

	“In 2016 I had the opportunity to live in Brazil for one year. At the time I was trying to work on this other project about Fukushima, but it wasn’t going well so I just decided to, you know, lay back and just have beers in the morning, etc.,” Matsubayashi says. “That’s when I actually found out about the forced relocation of Japanese Brazilians in Santos in Brazil.”

	That wartime relocation, in which some 60% of the Japanese immigrants forced out were from Okinawa, became the focus of Matsubayashi’s 2020 documentary “Okinawa/Santos.”

	“After that, I was exposed to the Urizunkai,” he says. “This is the Brazilian Okinawa community there, and so I happened to get to know them, and then I found out that they are sending Okinawa Brazilians to Okinawa for training and scholarship. So that’s actually the starting point of the project.”

	The Bunkyo, a cultural facility in São Paulo’s Liberdade district, a neighborhood with a particularly high concentration of Japanese immigrants, kept a vast and detailed library of immigrant documents in Portuguese and Japanese. It was an invaluable resource for Matsubayashi’s research, but the director also found inspiration in the sheer quantity of material, rather than just the data itself.
	

	“There’s a lot of documents for [immigrants] from the [other] 46 prefectures,” Matsubayashi says. The Okinawan records, he adds, came to almost the same volume. “Meaning that the Okinawans left a lot of records of themselves. I was really amazed at that vast amount of information that the Okinawans wanted to keep.”

	While making the 2020 film, Matsubayashi says, he was still an outsider, not being from Okinawa himself, but he became embedded in the community while filming interviews, and those interviews led to a deeper connection.

	“‘Ichariba choodee,’ that’s a [saying] in Okinawan dialect that means that [you are like] brother and sister, which [is how] they considered me once I interviewed them,” the director says.

	“I think that if I hadn’t developed ‘Okinawa/Santos’ as a film, I wouldn’t be able to have this film ‘Okinawa Saudade,’” he says. “When you’re there shooting you would need to get a coordinator, you need to get a driver, but I didn’t have to do that because they all arranged everything for me, and they worked as volunteers.”

	The Okinawan Brazilians treated him as one of their own, he adds.

	By 2024, Matsubayashi had heard that the Brazilian government would give the victims of the forced relocation a form of official apology that July, and that Okinawan Brazilians might receive scholarships for an exchange program, with training in September. The timing worked out. Brazil’s Amnesty Commission formally apologized that July for the state’s post-World War II persecution of Japanese immigrants.

	Matsubayashi built the film around a search for one’s roots, and chose to tell it through Okinawan dance. He draws a distinction between the dance in its “traditional” forms in Okinawa and the “Creative” forms that emerged later.

	“What we call the ‘Creative Eisa’ in Brazil, that started about 45 years ago, so I would think that they can say theirs is a tradition as well,” he says. “One difference between the traditional and the Creative Eisa is that [in] traditional Eisa you would use the sanshin musical instrument, and you would sing as well as dance. But with Creative Eisa, you don’t need to have the sanshin.”

	“I think this is a film that’s done in a first person perspective: of Yumi, Everton, and myself. I am also in the film asking [myself], ‘Who am I, what kind of person am I?’ So it’s three people trying to ask that question in the film,” the director says.
	

	It’s a rather intimate point of view for following his subjects as they navigate these cultural nuances.

	“In my other films too, you can hear my voice or you can maybe see one or two shots of myself, but not too many,” he says.

	“This film, ‘Okinawa Saudade,’ it’s more of a film about dancing – dancing means that there’s more emotion involved. I think ‘Okinawa/Santos,’ that one was more about putting together different testimonials, and so that’s a big difference there,” Matsubayashi says.

	He suggests the subject let him lean further into a more subjective kind of filmmaking.

	Matsubayashi says that with “Okinawa/Santos,” he was able to work on TV programs for NHK, Japan’s public broadcaster. “Once you do that, you get about JPY10 million [$63,000] for that, and then I would use that money to create my next film, so that would have been my cycle,” he says. “However, I guess because of the weak currency and because they don’t have a big budget anymore, [NHK is] struggling as well.”

	That has hit his own finances.

	“And if I didn’t have a grant from the Okinawa Prefecture, I wouldn’t be able to have done post-pro on ‘Okinawa Saudade,’” he says. “So I can say that Japanese documentaries, we’re going through a lot of difficult circumstances right now.”

schema.headline: ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Director Matsubayashi Yoju on a 10-Year Journey Tracing Brazilian Dancers’ Island Roots

title: ‘Tetsuo’ Director Tsukamoto Shinya on Staying Independent and Why He Can’t Pull Away From War Films
description: Beloved independent filmmaker Tsukamoto Shinya gave a masterclass at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF), speaking about the pivotal
body:
Beloved independent filmmaker Tsukamoto Shinya gave a masterclass at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF), speaking about the pivotal works of his career as well as his most recent film, the English-language feature “Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People?”

	Perhaps most famous overseas for his 1989 feature “Tetsuo: The Iron Man,” Tsukamoto spoke candidly about his preference for working outside the studio system as much as possible. Moderator Ichiyama Shozo, TIFF’s programming director, called “Tetsuo” a “shock,” not so much for its body horror as for the fact that a film of that quality could emerge from the Japanese independent film scene at the time.
	

	Tsukamoto recalled shooting the film on 16mm, before the era of digital VFX.

	“No CG. We had a little bit of tokusatsu [practical special effects] technology at the time but this didn’t use any of that, this used stuff which was thrown out on the street and we basically stuck it on [Taguchi Tomorowo]’s face,” the director said. Of the effect of Taguchi gliding through the streets, he said to “think of it as really rough stop motion.”

	The film took about a year to make, Tsukamoto said, though “the time we spent with the crew was shorter, a lot of the time towards the end I was working alone – like the sparks flying off at the end [of the clip], that was something I worked on alone.”

	The success of “Tetsuo,” he said, took him to film festivals overseas and led to his second feature, the horror film “Hiruko the Goblin,” now with a higher budget.

	“‘Tetsuo’ was being shown at the small theaters but we were getting attention because of the audience which came to watch, and I got the offer to make the film [‘Hiruko’],” he said.
	

	Asked by Ichiyama whether he felt more pressure making a larger-scale film, Tsukamoto said he mostly managed it, in part because of his time working in commercials.

	Ichiyama pointed out that Tsukamoto has consistently produced his films independently over the years, as with “Bullet Ballet” and “Tokyo Fist.”

	“I did receive offers [from studios] but I didn’t want to become a director for hire, I didn’t think that suited me, and there’s certain things you want to do as a filmmaker,” the director said. “You want to be able to play with the material to maintain that interest, that first impulse. Without that, because I’m not that strong-willed, I thought it would be very difficult to me. I think my impulse as a creator is stronger with my own material, which is why I went down that path.”

	Tsukamoto said his 2014 war film “Fires on the Plain,” based on a novel by Ooka Shohei that Ichikawa Kon had also adapted in 1959, was made independently. It was shot partly in the Philippines, partly in Okinawa and the rest in Saitama Prefecture.

	“Prior to this, although it was in the realm of indies, our crew had grown, and we had a wonderful system where we were able of course to pay the fees accordingly, and we did ‘Gemini’ with Sedic [International] and ‘[A] Snake of June,’ and ‘Nightmare Detective’ and ‘Tetsuo: The Bullet Man,’” Tsukamoto said. “Through this work my team at the company were always on the go and had grown but we were kind of at the point where we were at a standstill.”

	“Fires on the Plain” was a film he “had always wanted to adapt,” he said. “[I] wanted to do this from my teens to my 20s to my 30s, I went to the Philippines to try [to] finance it in my 40s, and in my 50s.”

	Determined to make the film, he went as far as trying self-distribution.

	“The people involved, it was hard work for them so I wouldn’t wanna do it again but it’s something I wanted to do for a long time. I thought it was something I could do myself with SNS [social media],” he said. “In the beginning I was thinking of showing it in a small amount of theaters.”

	He was eventually persuaded to show it in 80 cinemas, he said, starting with 40 and then expanding.

	Short on time, the talk skipped ahead to “Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People?,” Tsukamoto’s second English-language film after 2009’s “Tetsuo: The Bullet Man.” The film, which played in competition at Venice in September, follows Allen Nelson, a New Yorker who joins the Marines at 18 and is haunted by what he did in Vietnam. Rodney Hicks, Geoffrey Rush and Lily Franky are among the cast.
	

	Tsukamoto said he came across the story while making “Fires on the Plain,” but COVID-19 and then the Hollywood actors’ strike caused delays long enough that he released “Shadow of Fire,” originally planned for after “Mr. Nelson,” first. Altogether, the process took around seven years.

	After the abbreviated career talk, an audience Q&A delved a little more into Tsukamoto’s filmmaking philosophies and views on contemporary independent film.

	Asked for advice for young filmmakers, he said that in his youth, “because we were shooting on 8mm and 16mm film and we wanted to make a theatrical film,” a lot of the budget went to film processing. With digital, he said, that money can now go elsewhere.

	“Anything is a canvas now, [whether] it’s done by a grammar school student or Van Gogh,” he said, pointing to YouTube as a north star for what can be learned and accomplished without a budget.

	Asked about ideas for upcoming work, Tsukamoto returned to “Mr. Nelson.”

	“The theme of war wasn’t something that I was going to linger on this long, I was going to be happy just creating ‘Fires on the Plain,’” he said. “But it’s the state of the world which made me continue to focus on war.”

	The question referred to an earlier interview in which he had spoken about having new ideas he wanted to explore. “I think I made that comment wanting to alleviate some of the darkness I was experiencing,” Tsukamoto said. “I don’t think I can pry myself away from it.”

	Asked how he balances multiple roles behind the camera, Tsukamoto put it down partly to efficient communication, knowing exactly what to shoot, retake or cut, and to time management. But he said he also simply likes taking on those responsibilities.

	“Filmmaking is an accumulation of everything I love,” he said. That, rather than saving money, is why he gets involved on so many levels, though there are practical benefits too.

	“I studied art in high school and uni, and I love drawing. Once I became a filmmaker I stopped drawing but I’m using the same brainpower when coming up with composition and blocking,” he said. “It feels very close to drawing or painting to me.”

schema.headline: ‘Tetsuo’ Director Tsukamoto Shinya on Staying Independent and Why He Can’t Pull Away From War Films

title: Jon Stewart Slams Haley Stevens’ Mike Rogers Endorsement Ahead of Election Day
description: On Monday night’s episode of “The Daily Show,” Jon Stewart took aim at Michigan congresswoman Haley Stevens and her 11th-hour switch to endorse Rep
body:
On Monday night’s episode of “The Daily Show,” Jon Stewart took aim at Michigan congresswoman Haley Stevens and her 11th-hour switch to endorse Republican Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Election Day on Tuesday.

	Stewart spent much of the segment trying to trace how Stevens’ change of heart could have happened, given that she’d been “very clear” about her and El-Sayed’s “shared goal” of defeating Rogers. The host then cut to news clips of Stevens opposing Rogers and his political stances; “Mike Rogers has shown that he’s just going to go along with whatever Donald Trump does. He’s not going to speak out when erratic tariffs are impacting our auto industry,” she said. “Rogers is a nightmare.”
	

	Despite those assertions, Stevens endorsed Rogers on Sunday, seemingly filmed from her car. “Is her car in a ditch? Is she endorsing Mike Rogers after getting in a car accident?” asked Stewart. “Real quick, before I lose consciousness, I am endorsing the nightmare… This is like the most diabolical episode of ‘Fargo’ I’ve ever seen.”

	Perhaps her endorsement had to do with the fact that El-Sayed did not “welcome” her to his campaign, wondered Stewart. (Stevens recently said that she’s “never been invited” to one of his campaign events.) 

	“That says why you’re mad at Abdul, but not why you’re for Rogers. Rogers is — hold on, let me find a word. A nightmare,” continued Stewart, “who is against every principle that you’ve worked for your entire career. I mean, at least say you were visited by three ghosts who convinced you that it turns out people don’t need health insurance. This can’t really be about getting your feelings hurt.”
	

	Stewart also poked fun of Stevens’ chaotic CNN appearance on Sunday night, during which she spoke with Anderson Cooper about her endorsement. Stewart cut to one part of the segment, during which Anderson “sassed” Stevens. “You see what you just did there, Haley Stevens? Are you happy with yourself? You just turned Anderson Cooper into Andy Cohen. He didn’t want to sass. He’s a newsman… You gave him no choice but to sass.”

	Stewart also poked fun at Trump’s closing message before the midterms, during which he focused primarily on the Reflecting Pool he delivered the speech in front of, rather than important political topics voters should know about, said the host. (Trump described the Reflecting Pool as almost as tall as “two Empire State Buildings” before describing the bottom’s color as “a beautiful dark blue, very dark blue. They call it American black blue.”)

	“That was the president of the United States on the day before the midterms, choosing to make a speech at the reflecting pool to talk about the reflecting pool. No symbolism. No metaphor. metaphors. Just straight-up pool,” said Stewart. “That was Donald Trump’s ‘I had it cleaned speech,’ if you will.”

	Check out the entire monologue below.

schema.headline: Jon Stewart Slams Haley Stevens’ Mike Rogers Endorsement Ahead of Election Day

            The company Disney star Erik von Detten worked for when he allegedly played an "instrumental" role in finding customers to buy gold says it owes over $60 million to creditors ... TMZ learned.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Rosland Capital, where Erik worked for years, revealed the massive figure as part of its ongoing bankruptcy.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Rosland Capital listed debts of $63,695,061. The company's business involved selling precious metals to retail customers.
      

            As we previously reported, Rosland filed for bankruptcy months after the company and Erik were sued for elder abuse by a couple, Sheila Greenberg and Norman Greenberg. The couple claimed Erik worked for Rosland, where he sold them gold.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The couple said they bought the gold for over $2 million, but later learned it was only worth $1.3 million. The lawsuit claimed Erik of took advantage of the couple due to their age.
      
    
            Erik did not respond to the suit before the company filed for bankruptcy.
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, the creditors in the bankruptcy claim Erik has been a "roadblock" in obtaining information about Rosland. The case is ongoing.

title: Heidi Klum's Halloween Posts May Have Given Away 'The Batman: Part II' Details
description:
Heidi Klum
                          Halloween Posts Spoil 'Batman 2' Villains?!?
body:
Heidi Klum
                          Halloween Posts Spoil 'Batman 2' Villains?!?
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Some pretty major details for "The Batman: Part II" might've accidentally leaked ... and it's all thanks to Heidi Klum's Halloween costume.
      
    
            Here's the deal ... prosthetics expert Mike Marino -- the same guy who transformed Colin Farrell into The Penguin for the HBO series and the first "The Batman" film -- helped create Heidi's elaborate severed hand costume ... and his company may have leaked the villains for the upcoming film. 
      
    
            When prosthetics supplier The Makeup Armoury posted some behind-the-scenes photos, they seemed to be inadvertently revealing who Robert Pattison's Batman is up against. 
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Fans spotted some head casts on a shelf in the workshop -- noting one of them looked like "Game of Thrones" alum Charles Dance.
      
    
            Another one looked like Brian Tyree Henry. The head cast had a little scarring, which seems to give some legitimacy to rumors he'll be playing Two-Face in the film.
      
    
            Fans also noticed a face that looks an awful lot like Sebastian Stan, clocking that it was by a storage box that read, "Zsasz," the name of one of Batman's enemies.
      
    
            Stan, Charles and Brian's castings were all announced back in May ... but this is the first time we've gotten possible glimpses at their characters.

body:
Fatal Palm Beach Plane Crash
                          Victims Identified
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                November 2, 2026
                
                            11:42 AM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 2, 2026
                                4:33 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The passengers on the private jet that crashed in Florida have been identified ... they were a family of four from Texas ... and they were traveling with their nanny and two friends ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Onboard the Learjet 60 that crashed Sunday were 44-year-old Austin tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, plus his wife Helen, their two kids, and two close friends ... sources close to the family tell TMZ.
      
    
            The Robinsons had their nanny with them ... and the two pilots also died.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            We broke the story ... the captain was 55-year-old Jeff Gregory.
      
    
            His co-pilot was 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha. She earned her pilot's license when she was just 17 years old, doing so before she even graduated high school.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The private jet was flying from Austin to the Bahamas when it took a nosedive and crashed in Florida. Video shows the jet plummeting from the sky, nose-first, as it explodes on a busy street.
      
    
            The NTSB held a news conference Monday, confirming ice began forming on the jet in the middle of moderate turbulence. The crew asked to increase altitude from 35,000 feet to 37,000 feet shortly before an emergency was declared.
      
    
            RIP
